questions.question: One million random numbers are generated from a statistically stationary process with a Gaussian distribution with mean zero and standard deviation \(\sigma_0\). The \(\sigma_0\) is estimated by randomly drawing out \(10{,}000\) numbers of samples \((x_n)\). The estimates \(\hat{\sigma}_1\), \(\hat{\sigma}_2\) are computed in the following two ways. \[\hat{\sigma}_1^2=\frac{1}{10000}\sum_{n=1}^{10000}x_n^2\] \[\hat{\sigma}_2^2=\frac{1}{9999}\sum_{n=1}^{10000}x_n^2\] Which of the following statements is true?
questions.explanation:
Given, \[\hat{\sigma}_1^2=\frac{1}{10000}\sum_{n=1}^{10000}x_n^2\] and \[\hat{\sigma}_2^2=\frac{1}{9999}\sum_{n=1}^{10000}x_n^2\] Since the random process has mean zero and variance \(\sigma_0^2\), \[E(x_n^2)=\sigma_0^2\] Now, \[E(\hat{\sigma}_1^2) = E\left(\frac{1}{10000}\sum_{n=1}^{10000}x_n^2\right)\] Using linearity of expectation, \[E(\hat{\sigma}_1^2) = \frac{1}{10000}\sum_{n=1}^{10000}E(x_n^2)\] \[E(\hat{\sigma}_1^2) = \frac{1}{10000}\times10000\times\sigma_0^2\] \[E(\hat{\sigma}_1^2)=\sigma_0^2\] Also, \[E(\hat{\sigma}_2^2) = \frac{1}{9999}\sum_{n=1}^{10000}E(x_n^2)\] \[E(\hat{\sigma}_2^2) = \frac{10000}{9999}\sigma_0^2 \neq \sigma_0^2\] Hence, only option C is correct. \[\boxed{\text{(c) } E(\hat{\sigma}_1^2)=\sigma_0^2}\]
Key points
  • For zero-mean Gaussian random variables, \[E(x_n^2)=\sigma_0^2\]
  • Expectation is linear: \[E\left(\sum X_n\right)=\sum E(X_n)\]
  • \(\hat{\sigma}_1^2\) is an unbiased estimator of variance.

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: One million random numbers are generated from a statistically stationary process with a Gaussian distribution with mean zero and standard deviation \(\sigma_0\). The \(\sigma_0\) is estimated by randomly drawing out \(10,000\) numbers of samples (\(x_n\)). The estimates \(\widehat{\sigma}_1, \widehat{\sigma}_2\) are computed in the following two ways: \[\widehat{\sigma}_1^2 = \frac{1}{100000} \sum_{n=1}^{10000} x_n^2 \qquad \widehat{\sigma}_2^2 = \frac{1}{9999} \sum_{n=1}^{10000} x_n^2\] Which of the following statements is true?
questions.explanation:
We are given a statistically stationary process with a Gaussian distribution. The population parameters are: \[\text{Mean } \mu = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \text{Standard Deviation } = \sigma_0\] Since the mean is known to be exactly zero (\(\mu = 0\)), the true population variance is defined as the expectation of the squared samples: \[\sigma_0^2 = E(x_n^2) - \mu^2 = E(x_n^2) - 0 = E(x_n^2)\] Let us calculate the mathematical expectation of the first estimator \(\widehat{\sigma}_1^2\): \[\widehat{\sigma}_1^2 = \dfrac{1}{10000} \sum_{n=1}^{10000} x_n^2\] Take the expectation on both sides: \[\begin{aligned} E(\widehat{\sigma}_1^2) &= E\left( \dfrac{1}{10000} \sum_{n=1}^{10000} x_n^2 \right) \\[1.5ex] &= \dfrac{1}{10000} \sum_{n=1}^{10000} E(x_n^2) \\[1.5ex] &= \dfrac{1}{10000} \sum_{n=1}^{10000} \sigma_0^2 \\[1.5ex] &= \dfrac{1}{10000} \cdot \left(10000 \cdot \sigma_0^2\right) = \sigma_0^2 \end{aligned}\] Since \(E(\widehat{\sigma}_1^2) = \sigma_0^2\), the estimator \(\widehat{\sigma}_1^2\) is an unbiased estimator of the population variance. \[\boxed{\text{C. } E(\widehat{\sigma}_1^2) = \sigma_0^2}\]
Key points
  • Unbiased Variance Estimator with Known Mean: When the true population mean \(\mu\) is known exactly (here, \(\mu = 0\)), dividing the sum of squares by the full sample size \(N\) yields an unbiased estimator. The \((N-1)\) Bessel's correction factor is only required when the mean is unknown and must be approximated using the sample mean \(\bar{x}\).

questions.question: Three points in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane are \((-1, 0.8)\), \((0, 2.2)\) and \((1, 2.8)\). The value of the slope of the best fit straight line in the least square sense is (Round off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
We are given three data coordinates in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane: \[(-1, 0.8), \quad (0, 2.2), \quad (1, 2.8)\] We want to determine the slope (\(m\)) of the best-fit straight line \(y = mx + c\) using the method of least squares. Step 1: Compute the summary statistics Let us arrange the values into a summary table:
\(x\)\(y\)\(x^2\)\(xy\)
\(-1\)\(0.8\)\(1\)\(-0.8\)
\(0\)\(2.2\)\(0\)\(0.0\)
\(1\)\(2.8\)\(1\)\(2.8\)
\(\sum x = 0\)\(\sum y = 5.8\)\(\sum x^2 = 2\)\(\sum xy = 2.0\)
The sample size is \(N = 3\). Step 2: Apply the least-squares slope formula The normal equation for the slope parameter \(m\) is: \[m = \dfrac{N\sum xy - \left(\sum x\right)\left(\sum y\right)}{N\sum x^2 - \left(\sum x\right)^2}\] Substitute our summary statistics into the equation: \[m = \dfrac{3(2.0) - (0)(5.8)}{3(2) - (0)^2} = \dfrac{6.0}{6} = 1.00\] \[\boxed{1.00}\]
Key points
  • Symmetric Grid Simplification: When the independent data coordinates \(x\) are symmetrically centered around zero (\(\sum x = 0\)), the least-squares formula simplifies directly to: \[m = \dfrac{\sum xy}{\sum x^2}\]

questions.question: For the circuit shown in the figure, \(V_1 = 8\text{ V, DC}\) and \(I_1 = 8\text{ A, DC}\). The voltage \(V_{\text{ab}}\) in Volts is (Round off to 1 decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Given, \[V_1=8~\text{V}\] Choose node \(b\) as the reference node: \[V_b=0 \Rightarrow V_{N_3}=0\] Let the voltage at node \(a\) be \(V_a\). Then voltage at node \(N_1\) is \(8\,\text{V}\) (\(\because V_{N_3}=0\)). Applying KCL at node \(a\), \[\frac{V_a-8}{0.5} + \frac{V_a}{3} + \frac{V_a}{3} = 0\] Multiplying throughout by \(3\), \[6(V_a-8)+V_a+V_a=0\] \[6V_a-48+2V_a=0 \Rightarrow V_a=6~\text{V}\] Therefore, \[V_{ab}=V_a-V_b=6\]
Method 2
The two \(3\Omega\) resistors and the two \(2\Omega\) resistors are connected in parallel. Hence, \[R_{\text{eq}_3} = 3\parallel 3 = \frac{3\times3}{3+3} = 1.5\Omega, \qquad R_{\text{eq}_2} = 2\parallel 2 = 1\Omega\] Applying the Voltage Divider Rule, \[V_{ab} = \frac{1.5}{1.5+0.5}\times 8= 6~\text{V}\] Thus, \[\boxed{6.0}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: The value of parameters of the circuit shown in the figure are: \(R_1 = 2\ \Omega, R_2 = 2\ \Omega, R_3 = 3\ \Omega, L = 10\text{ mH}, C = 100\ \mu\text{F}\) For time \(t < 0\), the circuit is at steady state with the switch '\(\text{K}\)' in closed condition. If the switch is opened at \(t = 0\), the value of the voltage across the inductor (\(V_{\text{L}}\)) at \(t = 0^{+}\) in Volts is (Round off to 1 decimal place).
questions.explanation: For \(t<0\), the switch is closed and the circuit is in steady state. Hence, \[\text{Inductor} \rightarrow \text{short circuit}, \qquad \text{Capacitor} \rightarrow \text{open circuit}\] Therefore, the capacitor branch carries no current. The remaining circuit consists of \(R_1=2\Omega\) in parallel with \(R_3=3\Omega\), fed by the \(10~\text{A}\) current source. \[R_{eq} = R_1\parallel R_3 = \frac{2\times3}{2+3} = 1.2\Omega\] Hence, the voltage across the parallel network is \[V_2=V_3 = 10\times1.2 = 12~\text{V}\] Therefore, \[i_L(0^-) = \frac{12}{2} = 6~\text{A}\] and \[v_C(0^-) = 12~\text{V}\] Using continuity of inductor current and capacitor voltage, \[i_L(0^+) = i_L(0^-) = 6~\text{A}, \qquad v_C(0^+) = v_C(0^-) = 12~\text{V}\] After the switch is opened, \(R_3\) is disconnected. At \(t=0^+\), the inductor behaves as a \(6~\text{A}\) current source and the capacitor behaves as a \(12~\text{V}\) voltage source. Current through \(R_1\) is, \(i_1=6~\text{A}\) Hence, the voltage drop across \(R_1\) is \[V_{R_1} = i_1R_1 = 6\times2 = 12~\text{V}\] Let \(V\) be the potential across 10A source. The current through \(R_2\) is \[i_2 = \frac{V-12}{2}\] Also, \[i_1+i_2=10\] \[6+\frac{V-12}{2}=10\] \[V=20~\text{V}\] Applying KVL, \[V = V_{R_1}+V_L\] \[20 = 12+V_L \ \Rightarrow \ V_L=8~\text{V}\] Hence, \[\boxed{8.0}\]

questions.ref: 2nd Order Dynamics and Complex Impedance Q1
questions.question: The circuit shown in the figure is initially in the steady state with the switch K in open condition and \(\overline{K}\)in closed condition. The switch K is closed and \(\overline{K}\) is opened simultaneously at the instant \(t=t_1\) where \(t_1>0\). The minimum value of \(t_1\) in milliseconds such that there is no transient in the voltage across the \(100\,\mu\text{F}\) capacitor is (Round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation: Before \(t = t_{1}\), switch \(K\) is open and switch \(\overline{K}\) is closed. The circuit has reached steady state under the excitation of the AC current source and the DC voltage source. The capacitive reactance is calculated as: \[X_{c} = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{1000 \times 100 \times 10^{-6}} = 10\,\Omega\] In this state, the current from the \(5\,\text{V}\) DC source keeps circulating in its own local loop through \(\overline{K}\) and does not affect the capacitor. Thus, the steady-state voltage \(V_c\) across the capacitor due to the AC source (\(1\angle 0^\circ\,\text{A}\) at \(\omega = 1000\,\text{rad/s}\)) is: \[{V}_{c} = 1\angle 0^\circ \cdot [10 \parallel (-j10)] = 1\angle 0^\circ \cdot \left( \frac{-j100}{10 - j10} \right) = \frac{10}{\sqrt{2}}\angle -45^\circ\,\text{V}\] Converting this to the time-domain expression for the capacitor voltage gives: \[v_{c}(t) = \frac{10}{\sqrt{2}} \sin(1000t - 45^\circ)\] At \(t = t_{1}\), the initial voltage across the capacitor is: \[v_{c}(t_{1}) = \frac{10}{\sqrt{2}} \sin(1000t_{1} - 45^\circ)\] After \(t = t_{1}\), switch \(K\) is closed (shorting the AC current source and the \(10\,\Omega\) parallel resistor) and switch \(\bar{K}\) is opened. This configures a series \(RC\) circuit connected to the \(5\,\text{V}\) DC source. The parameters for this new configuration are: \[\text{Steady-state capacitor voltage, } V_{ss} = 5\,\text{V}\] \[\text{Time constant, } \tau = R C = 10\,\Omega \times 100\,\mu\text{F} = 1000\,\mu\text{s} = 1\,\text{ms}\] The complete voltage response across the capacitor for \(t \ge t_{1}\) is given by: \[v_{c}(t) = V_{ss} + [v_{c}(t_{1}) - V_{ss}] e^{-(t - t_{1})/\tau}\] \[v_{c}(t) = 5 + \left[ \frac{10}{\sqrt{2}} \sin(1000t_{1} - 45^\circ) - 5 \right] e^{-(t - t_{1})/\tau}\] The second term in the expression represents the transient response. For a transient-free response, the coefficient of the exponential term must equal zero: \[\frac{10}{\sqrt{2}} \sin(1000t_{1} - 45^\circ) - 5 = 0\] \[\sin\left(1000t_{1} - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{5}{\frac{10}{\sqrt{2}}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\] Taking the appropriate principal angle to solve for the timing condition: \[1000t_{1} - \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{4}\] \[1000t_{1} = \frac{\pi}{2}\] \[t_{1} = \frac{\pi}{2000}\,\text{s} = \frac{\pi}{2}\,\text{ms} \approx 1.57\,\text{ms}\] \[\boxed{1.57}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: For the circuit shown, if \(i=\sin1000t\), the instantaneous value of the Thevenin’s equivalent voltage (in Volts) across the terminals a-b at time t = 5 ms is (Round off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Let node \(b\) be selected as the reference ground node (\(V_{b} = 0\,\text{V}\)). Thus, the node voltages can be defined relative to node \(b\) as \(V_{ab}\) and \(V_{cb}\). From the circuit diagram, the relationship across the dependent voltage source is: \[V_{ab} = V_{cb} + 4\,i_{x}\] The current \(i_{x}\) flowing through the left branch is given by: \[i_{x} = \frac{V_{ab}}{10 - j10}\] Substituting \(V_{ab}\) into the equation for \(i_{x}\): \[i_{x}(10 - j10) = V_{cb} + 4\,i_{x}\] \[i_{x}(6 - j10) = V_{cb} \implies i_{x} = \frac{V_{cb}}{6 - j10}\] Writing the nodal analysis equation at node \(c\) (supernode structure combined with the independent current source entering the node): \[-1\angle 0^{\circ} + \frac{V_{cb}}{10 + j10} + \frac{V_{ab}}{10 - j10} = 0\] Substituting \(V_{ab} = V_{cb} + 4\,i_{x}\) into the nodal equation: \[\frac{V_{cb}}{10 + j10} + \frac{V_{cb} + 4\,i_{x}}{10 - j10} = 1\] \[V_{cb}\left(\frac{1}{10 + j10} + \frac{1}{10 - j10}\right) + \frac{4}{10 - j10}\left(\frac{V_{cb}}{6 - j10}\right) = 1\] \[V_{cb}\left(\frac{1}{10 + j10} + \frac{1}{10 - j10} + \frac{4}{(10 - j10)(6 - j10)}\right) = 1\] Solving this complex algebraic equation yields: \[V_{cb} = 10 - j2.5\,\text{V}\] Using the relationship found for \(i_{x}\): \[i_{x} =\frac{V_{cb}}{6 - j10}= 0.625 + j0.625\,\text{A}\] Now, calculating the terminal voltage \(V_{ab}\): \[V_{ab} = V_{cb} + 4\,i_{x}= 12.5\angle 0^{\circ}\,\text{V} = 12.5\sin(\omega t)\,\text{V}\] Evaluating the instantaneous voltage at \(t = 5\,\text{ms}\) as shown in the derivation: \[V_{ab} = -11.98\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{-11.98}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not treat the dependent voltage source as an independent node; its constraint equation (\(V_{ab} - V_{cb} = 4\,i_{x}\)) must be explicitly maintained.

questions.question: The admittance parameters of the passive resistive two-port network shown in the figure are: \(y_{11} = 5\,\text{S}, y_{22} = 1\,\text{S}, y_{12} = y_{21} = -2.5\,\text{S}\) The power delivered to the load resistor \(R_L\) in Watt is (Round off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
The two-port admittance parameters are provided as: \[[Y]_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2.5 \\ -2.5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] A \(3\,\Omega\) resistor is connected in parallel to this two-port network. For the \(3\,\Omega\) parallel resistor element, the terminal currents are given by: \[I_1 = \frac{V_1 - V_2}{3}\] \[I_2 = \frac{V_2 - V_1}{3}\] Thus, the admittance matrix for the \(3\,\Omega\) parallel branch is: \[[Y]_2 = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \end{bmatrix}\] For parallel networks, the overall equivalent \(Y\)-parameters are obtained by adding the individual \(Y\)-parameters: \[[Y]_{eq} = [Y]_1 + [Y]_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 5 + \frac{1}{3} & -2.5 - \frac{1}{3} \\ -2.5 - \frac{1}{3} & 1 + \frac{1}{3} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{16}{3} & -\frac{17}{6} \\ -\frac{17}{6} & \frac{4}{3} \end{bmatrix}\] The resulting network equations are: \[I_1 = \frac{16}{3}V_1 - \frac{17}{6}V_2 \quad \text{--- (1)}\] \[I_2 = -\frac{17}{6}V_1 + \frac{4}{3}V_2 \quad \text{--- (2)}\] Given that the input voltage \(V_1 = 10\,\text{V}\) and the network is terminated by a load resistance \(R_L = 6\,\Omega\), the output terminal voltage is: \[V_2 = -I_2 R_L = -6I_2\] Substituting \(V_1 = 20\,\text{V}\) and \(V_2 = -6I_2\) into equation (2): \[I_2 = -\frac{17}{6}(20) + \frac{4}{3}(-6I_2)\] \[I_2 = -\frac{170}{3} - 8I_2\] \[9I_2 = -\frac{170}{3}\] \[I_2 = -\frac{170}{27} \,\text{A}\] The power delivered to the load resistor \(R_L\) is given by: \[\text{Power} = I_2^2 R_L = \left(-\frac{170}{27}\right)^2 \times 6 \approx 238\,\text{W}\]
Key points
  • When two two-port networks are connected in parallel, their individual admittance matrix parameters (\(Y\)-parameters) are directly added to determine the equivalent network response.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not omit the negative sign in the terminal relation \(V_2 = -I_2 R_L\), as the standard two-port parameter currents are defined as entering the network ports.
\[\boxed{238}\]

questions.question:
The period of the discrete time signal \(x[n]\) described by the equation below is \(N = \underline{\hspace{1.5cm}}\) (Round off to the nearest integer). \[x[n] = 1 + 3\sin\left(\frac{15\pi}{8}n + \frac{3\pi}{4}\right)
       - 5\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}n - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\]
questions.explanation: The given discrete-time signal is \[x[n]=1+3\sin\left(\frac{15\pi}{8}n+\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)-5\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}n-\frac{\pi}{4}\right).\] The constant term is periodic for every integer \(N\). For a discrete-time sinusoid with frequency \(\omega\), the fundamental period is the smallest positive integer \(N\) satisfying \[\omega N=2\pi k,\qquad k\in\mathbb{Z}.\] For the first sinusoid, \[\omega_1=\frac{15\pi}{8},\] \[N_1=\frac{2\pi}{15\pi/8}k=\frac{16}{15}k.\] The smallest integer value is obtained for \(k=15\): \[N_1=16.\] For the second sinusoid, \[\omega_2=\frac{\pi}{3},\] \[N_2=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/3}=6.\] Hence, the fundamental period of the sum is \[N=\operatorname{LCM}(16,6)=48.\] Therefore, \[\boxed{48}\]

questions.question: For the signals \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\) shown in the figure, \(z(t) = x(t) * y(t)\) is maximum at \(t = T_1\). Then \(T_1\) in seconds is \(\underline{\hspace{1.5cm}}\) (Round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
The signals are \[x(t)=
\begin{cases}
1, & -1\le t\le 1,\\
0, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}\] and \[y(t)=
\begin{cases}
t-3, & 1\le t\le 5,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}\] Since \(x(t)\) is a unit rectangular pulse of width \(2\), \[z(t)=x(t)*y(t)
=\int_{-1}^{1}y(t-\tau)\,d\tau
=\int_{t-1}^{t+1}y(u)\,du.\] Thus, \(z(t)\) equals the area under \(y(u)\) over a sliding window of width \(2\). Evaluating, \[z(t)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{t^{2}}{2}-2t+\dfrac{3}{2}, & 0\le t\le 2,\\ 2t-6, & 2\le t\le 4,\\ -\dfrac{t^{2}}{2}+4t-4, & 4\le t\le 6.
\end{cases}\] For the last interval, \[\frac{dz(t)}{dt}=4-t.\] Hence, \[\frac{dz(t)}{dt}=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
T_{1}=4~\text{s}.\] \[\boxed{4}\]

The maximum frequency present in the filtered signal, in \(\mathrm{Hz}\) is . (Round off to the nearest integer.)
questions.explanation:
Using the trigonometric identity, \[2\cos A \cos B=\cos(A+B)+\cos(A-B),\] the given signal becomes \[x(t)=\cos(240\pi t)+\cos(120\pi t).\] Hence, the original frequency components are \[f_1=\frac{240\pi}{2\pi}=120\,\text{Hz}, \qquad
f_2=\frac{120\pi}{2\pi}=60\,\text{Hz}.\] The sampling frequency is \[f_s=200\,\text{Hz}, \qquad \frac{f_s}{2}=100\,\text{Hz}.\] The \(60\,\text{Hz}\) component lies below the Nyquist frequency and remains unchanged. The \(120\,\text{Hz}\) component aliases to \[f_a=\left|f_s-120\right|
=\left|200-120\right|
=80\,\text{Hz}.\] Therefore, after sampling, the spectrum contains frequency components at \[60\,\text{Hz}\quad \text{and}\quad 80\,\text{Hz}.\] An ideal low-pass filter with cutoff frequency \(100\,\text{Hz}\) passes both components. Hence, the maximum frequency present in the filtered signal is \[\boxed{80}\]

questions.question: The \(Z\)-transform of a discrete signal \(x[n]\) is \[X(z)=\frac{4z}{\left(z-\frac{1}{5}\right)\left(z-\frac{2}{3}\right)(z-3)}\] with ROC \(=R\). Which one of the following statements is true?
options: Discrete-time Fourier transform of \(x[n]\) converges if \(R\) is \(|z|>3\).
Discrete-time Fourier transform of \(x[n]\) converges if \(R\) is \(\dfrac{2}{3}<|z|<3\).
Discrete-time Fourier transform of \(x[n]\) converges if \(R\) is such that \(x[n]\) is a left-sided sequence.
Discrete-time Fourier transform of \(x[n]\) converges if \(R\) is such that \(x[n]\) is a right-sided sequence.
questions.explanation:
The discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT) exists only if the unit circle \[|z|=1\] lies in the region of convergence (ROC) of the Z-transform. The poles of \[X(z)=\frac{4z}{\left(z-\frac{1}{5}\right)\left(z-\frac{2}{3}\right)(z-3)}\] are at \[z=\frac{1}{5},\quad \frac{2}{3},\quad 3.\] Possible ROCs are \[|z|>3,\qquad
\frac{2}{3}<|z|<3,\qquad
\frac{1}{5}<|z|<\frac{2}{3},\qquad
|z|<\frac{1}{5}.\] Among these, only \[\frac{2}{3}<|z|<3\] contains the unit circle \((|z|=1)\). Hence, the DTFT exists only for this ROC. \[\boxed{\textbf{(b) DTFT of }x[n]\textbf{ converges if }R\textbf{ is }\frac{2}{3}<|z|<3.}\]

When switch \(S\) is ON, \(D_1\) conducts and both \(D_2\) and \(D_3\) are reverse biased

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: Consider the OP AMP based circuit shown in the figure. Ignore the conduction drops of diodes \(D_1\) and \(D_2\). All the components are ideal and the breakdown voltage of the Zener is \(5\text{ V}\). Which of the following statements is true?
options: The maximum and minimum values of the output voltage \(V_O\) are \(+15\text{ V}\) and \(-10\text{ V}\), respectively.
The maximum and minimum values of the output voltage \(V_O\) are \(+5\text{ V}\) and \(-15\text{ V}\), respectively.
The maximum and minimum values of the output voltage \(V_O\) are \(+10\text{ V}\) and \(-5\text{ V}\), respectively.
The maximum and minimum values of the output voltage \(V_O\) are \(+5\text{ V}\) and \(-10\text{ V}\), respectively.
questions.explanation:
The input voltage is \(V_{\text{in}} = 10\sin(1000t)\,\text{V}\). To find the behavior, we analyze the circuit during each half-cycle of the input: 1. Positive Half-Cycle (\(V_{\text{in}} > 0\)):
  • Initially, the inverting node voltage \(V_-\) rises above \(V_+ = 0\,\text{V}\), driving the op-amp output to negative saturation (\(V_O = -V_{\text{sat}}\)).
  • img/ch3_operational_amplifier/3_23_1_A.png
  • Diode \(D_1\) and the Zener diode \(D_z\) are forward-biased, while \(D_2\) is reverse-biased.
  • A negative feedback path is established through the \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor and \(D_1\).
  • The circuit acts as an inverting amplifier: \[V_O = -\left(\frac{1\,\text{k}\Omega}{1\,\text{k}\Omega}\right) V_{\text{in}} = -V_{\text{in}}\]
  • Since \(V_{\text{in, max}} = +10\,\text{V}\), the minimum output voltage is: \[V_{O,\text{min}} = -10\,\text{V}\]
2. Negative Half-Cycle (\(V_{\text{in}} < 0\)):
  • The inverting node voltage \(V_-\) falls below \(0\,\text{V}\), driving the output to positive saturation (\(V_O = +V_{\text{sat}}\)).
  • img/ch3_operational_amplifier/3_23_1_B.png
  • Diode \(D_2\) becomes forward-biased, whereas \(D_1\) and \(D_z\) are reverse-biased.
  • The Zener diode \(D_z\) enters breakdown (\(V_z = 5\,\text{V}\)).
  • The feedback path clamps the output voltage relative to the virtual ground (\(V_- = 0\,\text{V}\)): \[V_O = V_- + V_z = 0 + 5\,\text{V} = +5\,\text{V}\]
  • Thus, the maximum output voltage is: \[V_{O,\text{max}} = +5\,\text{V}\]
\[\boxed{\text{(D) The maximum and minimum values of the output voltage $V_O$ are $+5\text{ V}$ and $-10\text{ V}$, respectively.}}\]
Key points
Zener Breakdown vs Forward Bias: An ideal Zener diode acts as a closed switch (short circuit) when forward-biased, and maintains a constant breakdown voltage \(V_z\) when reverse-biased with sufficient voltage.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: Neglecting the delays due to the logic gates in the circuit shown in figure, the decimal equivalent of the binary sequence \([ABCD]\) of initial logic states, which will not change with clock, is
questions.explanation:
Given: Sequential circuit containing two D flip-flops labeled \(Q_2\) (left) and \(Q_1\) (right), a NOR gate configured as an inverter, and an XOR gate. 1. Expressing Node Logic Equations: From the circuit topology, the combinational nodes are expressed in terms of the flip-flop states as follows:
  • Node \(A\) is connected to the inverted output of the left flip-flop: \(A = \overline{Q}_2\).
  • Node \(B\) is the output of the NOR inverter fed by \(A\): \(B = \overline{A} = Q_2\).
  • Node \(C\) is the direct output of the left flip-flop: \(C = Q_2\).
  • Node \(D\) is the output of the XOR gate: \(D = B \oplus C = Q_2 \oplus Q_1\).
2. Setting Up Flip-Flop Input Equations: Looking closely at the routing to the \(D\) inputs of each flip-flop:
  • The left flip-flop input is driven by \(C\): \(D_2 = Q_1\).
  • The right flip-flop input is driven by \(D\): \(D_1 = D = Q_2 \oplus Q_1\).
3. Verifying the Stability (Fixed-Point) Condition: For a state to not change with the application of a clock pulse, the next-state equations must satisfy \(Q_{2,\text{next}} = Q_2\) and \(Q_{1,\text{next}} = Q_1\): \[Q_{2,\text{next}} = D_2 = Q_1 \implies Q_2 = Q_1\] \[Q_{1,\text{next}} = D_1 = Q_2 \oplus Q_1 \implies Q_1 = Q_2 \oplus Q_1\] Substituting \(Q_2 = Q_1\) into the second condition: \[Q_1 = Q_1 \oplus Q_1 \implies Q_1 = 0\] Since \(Q_2 = Q_1\), we find that the stable internal state is: \[Q_2 Q_1 = 00\] 4. Finding the Decimal Equivalent of \([ABCD]\): Substitute the stable state values (\(Q_2 = 0, Q_1 = 0\)) back into the sequence variables:
  • \(A = \overline{Q}_2 = \overline{0} = 1\)
  • \(B = Q_2 = 0\)
  • \(C = Q_1 = 0\)
  • \(D = B \oplus C = 0 \oplus 0 = 0\)
This yields the binary sequence: \[[ABCD] = 1000_2\] Converting this binary value to decimal: \[1000_2 = 1 \times 2^3 = 8\]
Key points
  • A sequential system is in a stable state (fixed point) when the values present at the \(D\) inputs match the current outputs (\(Q\)) before the clock edge arrives.
  • Correctly mapping the layout connections avoids false contradictions when setting up next-state balance equations.
8

questions.explanation: By Mason's gain formula, \[\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{P_{1}\Delta_{1} + P_{2}\Delta_{2}}{\Delta}\] Here, the forward path gains and their respective cofactor determinants are: \[P_{1} = 3,\ \Delta_{1} = 1\ \ \ \ \ \ ; \quad P_{2} = \frac{2}{s}, \ \Delta_{2} = 1\] The system determinant (\(\Delta\)) considering the feedback loop is: \(\Delta = 1 - \dfrac{1}{s}\) \[\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{3 + \dfrac{2}{s}}{1 - \dfrac{1}{s}} = \frac{3s + 2}{s - 1}\] \[\boxed{(B) \ \ \frac{3s + 2}{s - 1}}\]

questions.question: In the Nyquist plot of the open-loop transfer function \[G(s)H(s)=\frac{3s+5}{s-1}\] corresponding to the feedback loop shown in the figure, the infinite semi-circular arc of the Nyquist contour in \(s\)-plane is mapped into a point at

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: Consider a unity-gain negative feedback system consisting of the plant \(G(s)\) (given below) and a proportional-integral controller. Let the proportional gain and integral gain be \(3\) and \(1\), respectively. For a unit step reference input, the final values of the controller output and the plant output, respectively, are \[G(s)=\frac{1}{s-1}\]
questions.explanation: Given, \[G(s)=\frac{1}{s-1}\] The proportional gain and integral gain of the PI controller be \(K_P\) and \(K_I\) respectively. Thus, \[K_P=3,\qquad K_I=1\] Therefore, \[C(s)=K_P+\frac{K_I}{s}=3+\frac{1}{s}=\frac{3s+1}{s}\] Let the block diagram be, The open-loop transfer function is \[C(s)G(s) = \frac{3s+1}{s(s-1)}\] For a unit-gain negative feedback system, \[\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{C(s)G(s)}{1+C(s)G(s)} = \frac{\dfrac{3s+1}{s(s-1)}}{1+\dfrac{3s+1}{s(s-1)}} = \frac{3s+1}{(s+1)^2}\] For a unit step input, \(R(s)=\dfrac{1}{s}\), hence \[Y(s) = \frac{3s+1}{s(s+1)^2}\] Using the Final Value Theorem, \[y(\infty) = \lim_{s\to 0}sY(s) = \lim_{s\to 0}\frac{3s+1}{(s+1)^2}=1\] The controller output is \[U(s)=C(s)(R(s)-Y(s)) =\frac{3s+1}{s(s-1)}\times(\frac{1}{s}-\frac{3s+1}{s(s+1)^2})=\frac{(3s+1)(s-1)}{s(s+1)^2}\] Again using the Final Value Theorem, \[u(\infty) = \lim_{s\to 0}sU(s) = \lim_{s\to 0} \frac{(3s+1)(s-1)}{(s+1)^2}=-1\] Therefore, the final values of controller output and plant output are \[u(\infty)=-1, \qquad y(\infty)=1\] \[\boxed{\text{(D)}\;-1,\;1}\]

questions.question: Consider a lead compensator of the form \[K(s)=\frac{1+\dfrac{s}{a}}{1+\dfrac{s}{\beta a}},\ ~~~\beta>1,\ a>0\] The frequency at which this compensator produces maximum phase lead is \(4\,\text{rad/s}\). At this frequency, the gain amplification provided by the controller, assuming asymptotic Bode-magnitude plot of \(K(s)\), is \(6\,\text{dB}\). The values of \(a,\beta\), respectively, are
questions.explanation:
Given lead compensator, \[K(s)
=
\frac{1+\dfrac{s}{a}}{1+\dfrac{s}{\beta a}},
\qquad
\beta>1,~\text{a}>1\] For a lead compensator, the frequency at which maximum phase lead occurs is \[\omega_m=a\sqrt{\beta}\] Given, \[\omega_m=4~\text{rad/s}\] Therefore, \[a\sqrt{\beta}=4\] \[a^2\beta=16\] Also, the gain amplification provided by the compensator at \(\omega_m\) is \(20\log_{10}\left(\sqrt{\beta}\right)\) Given gain amplification is \(6\,\text{dB}\), \[20\log_{10}\left(\sqrt{\beta}\right)=6\] \[\beta\approx 4\] Thus \[a\sqrt{\beta}=4,\] \[a(2)=4\] \[a=2\] \[\boxed{\text{(B)}\;2,\;4}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: In the figure, the electric field \(E\) and the magnetic field \(B\) point to \(x\) and \(z\) directions, respectively, and have constant magnitudes. A positive charge `\(q\)' is released from rest at the origin. Which of the following statement(s) is/are true? [figure unavailable]
options: The charge will move in the direction of \(z\) with constant velocity.
The charge will always move on the \(y\)-\(z\) plane only.
The trajectory of the charge will be a circle.
The charge will progress in the direction of \(y\).
questions.explanation:
The net force acting on a charged particle in the presence of electric and magnetic fields is \[\vec{F} = q\vec{E} + q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\] Initially, the particle is at rest. Therefore, \[\vec{F}_m = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B}) = 0\] Hence, only the electric force acts on the particle. The electric field is along the \(+z\) direction; therefore, the particle starts accelerating upward. As the velocity increases, the magnetic force appears and acts perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity. Consequently, the direction of motion continuously changes while the electric field keeps accelerating the particle. The combined action of the two fields produces a cycloidal trajectory as shown in the figure. [figure unavailable] \[\vec{F}_e=q\vec{E}\] \[\vec{F}_m=q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\] At the cusps of the cycloid, \[v=0\] At the highest point of each loop, the speed becomes maximum: \[v=v_{\max}\] Hence, only statements (B) and (D) are consistent with the figure. \[\boxed{\text{B,D}}\]
Key points
  • Lorentz force is given by \(\vec{F}=q\vec{E}+q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\).
  • Magnetic force is always perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity.
  • A charged particle starting from rest experiences only electric force initially.
  • Crossed electric and magnetic fields can produce cycloidal motion.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume the magnetic force acts when the particle is initially at rest.
  • Remember that the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity.
  • Do not confuse cycloidal motion with circular or helical motion.
  • The electric field changes the particle's speed, whereas the magnetic field changes only its direction.

questions.subject: electrical-machines
questions.question: When the winding \(c\)-\(d\) of the single-phase \(50\text{ Hz}\) two winding transformer is supplied from an AC current source of frequency \(50\text{ Hz}\), the rated voltage of \(200\text{ V}\) (rms) \(50\text{ Hz}\) is obtained at the open-circuit terminals \(a\)-\(b\). The cross sectional area of the core is \(5000\text{ mm}^2\) and the average length of the core traversed by the mutual flux is \(500\text{ mm}\).The maximum allowable flux density in the core is \(B_{max} = 1\text{ Wb/m}^2\) and the relative permeability of the core material is \(5000\). The leakage impedance of the winding \(a\)-\(b\) and the winding \(c\)-\(d\) in \(50\text{ Hz}\) are \((5 + j100\pi \times 0.16)\text{ }\Omega\) and \((11.25 + j100\pi \times 0.36)\text{ }\Omega\), respectively. Considering the magnetizing characteristics to be linear and neglecting core loss, the self-inductance of the winding \(a\)-\(b\) in millihenry is (round to the 1 decimal place). [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
Given:
  • Open circuit voltage across terminals \(a\)-\(b\) is \(200\,\text{V}\) (rms)
  • Frequency: \[f = 50\,\text{Hz}\]
  • Maximum flux density relation: \[\phi_{m} = 5000 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{Wb}\]
  • Relative permeability: \[\mu_{r} = 5000\]
  • Leakage inductance of primary: \[L_{\ell p} = 0.16\,\text{H}\]
Using the emf equation of transformer:\[E = 4.44 f N \phi_{m}\]Substituting the given values:\[200 = 4.44 \times 50 \times N_{1} \times 5000 \times 10^{-6}\]\[N_{1} = 180 \text{ turns}\]Reluctance of flux path inside the core is:\[\mathcal{R} = \frac{\ell}{\mu_{0}\mu_{r}A}\]Substituting the values:\[\mathcal{R}=\frac{0.5}{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 5000 \times 5000 \times 10^{-6}}=15915.494\,\text{A-T/Wb}\]Mutual inductance referred to primary:\[M = \frac{N_{1}^{2}}{\mathcal{R}}\]\[M=\frac{(180)^{2}}{15915.494}=2.0357\,\text{H}\]Self inductance of primary:\[L_{p} = M + L_{\ell p}\]\[L_{p} = 2.0357 + 0.16 = 2.1957\,\text{H}\]\[L_{p} = 2195.7\,\text{mH}\]\[\boxed{2195.7}\]
Key points
  • Transformer emf equation: \[E = 4.44 f N \phi_{m}\]
  • Mutual inductance is related to reluctance by: \[M = \frac{N^{2}}{\mathcal{R}}\]
  • Self inductance includes both mutual and leakage inductance components.

questions.explanation:
Magnetic field produced by stator is as shown in the figure. [figure unavailable] Number of poles, \[P=4\] Relation between electrical and mechanical angle is \[\theta_e=\frac{P}{2}\theta_m\] \[\theta_m=\frac{2}{P}\theta_e\] Given, \[\theta_e=90^\circ\] \[\theta_m=\frac{2}{4}\times 90^\circ=45^\circ\] Thus, geometrical neutral axis lies at \(90^\circ\) electrical from pole axis, i.e. \(45^\circ\) mechanical from pole axis. questions.question: A separately excited DC motor rated \(400\,\text{V}\), \(15\,\text{A}\), \(1500\,\text{RPM}\) drives a constant torque load at rated speed operating from \(400\,\text{V}\) DC supply drawing rated current. The armature resistance is \(1.2\,\Omega\). If the supply voltage drops by \(10\%\) with field current unaltered then the resultant speed of the motor in RPM is (Round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Load torque is constant, \[T=\text{constant}\] Under rated condition, \[E_1=V_t-I_ar_a\] \[E_1=400-(15)(1.2)=382\,\text{V}\] Since the motor is separately excited, \[\phi=\text{constant}\] When supply voltage is reduced by \(10\%\), \[V_{t2}=400-400\times\frac{10}{100}=360\,\text{V}\] For constant torque, \[T\propto \phi I_a\] Since \(\phi\) is constant, \[I_a=\text{constant}=15\,\text{A}\] \[E_2=V_{t2}-I_ar_a\] \[E_2=360-(15)(1.2)=342\,\text{V}\] As \(\phi=\text{constant}\), \[E\propto N\] \[\frac{E_2}{E_1}=\frac{N_2}{N_1}\] \[\frac{342}{382}=\frac{N_2}{1500}\] \[N_2=1343\,\text{rpm}\] \[\boxed{1343}\]
Key points
  • For a separately excited DC motor, flux remains constant if field excitation is unchanged.
  • For constant torque, armature current remains constant.
  • Speed is proportional to back emf when flux is constant.

questions.question: A three phase \(415\text{ V}\), \(50\text{ Hz}\), \(6\)-pole, \(960\text{ RPM}\), \(4\text{ HP}\) squirrel cage induction motor drives a constant torque load at rated speed operating from rated supply and delivering rated output. If the supply voltage and frequency are reduced by \(20\%\), the resultant speed of the motor in \(\text{RPM}\) (neglecting the stator leakage impedance and rotational losses) is (Round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Given that both voltage and frequency are reduced by \(20\%\), \[\frac{V}{f}=\text{constant}\] The motor drives a constant torque load. Hence, \[N_{s}-N_{r}=\text{constant}\] Initially, \[f_{1}=50\,\text{Hz}\] After a \(20\%\) reduction, \[f_{2}=50-\frac{20}{100}\times 50=40\,\text{Hz}\] For a \(6\)-pole motor, \[N_{s1}=\frac{120\times 50}{6}=1000\,\text{rpm}\] \[N_{s2}=\frac{120\times 40}{6}=800\,\text{rpm}\] Using the constant torque condition, \[N_{s1}-N_{r1}=N_{s2}-N_{r2}\] \[1000-960=800-N_{r2}\] \[N_{r2}=760\,\text{rpm}\] \[\boxed{760}\]
Key points
  • For constant flux operation in V/f control, \(\dfrac{V}{f}\) is maintained constant.
  • For a constant torque load, slip speed \((N_s-N_r)\) remains approximately constant.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume slip remains constant; slip speed remains constant for constant torque operation.
  • Use the reduced frequency to calculate the new synchronous speed.

questions.question: A three-phase synchronous motor with synchronous impedance of \(0.1 + j0.3\) per unit per phase has a static stability limit of \(2.5\) per unit. The corresponding excitation voltage in per unit is (Round off to \(2\) decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Given, \[Z_s=(0.1+j0.3)\] \[|Z_s| = \sqrt{0.1^2+0.3^2} = 0.3162\] \[\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{0.3}{0.1}\right) = 71.56^\circ\] Hence, \[Z_s=0.3162\angle 71.56^\circ \;\text{p.u.}\] The developed power is maximum when \[\delta=\theta\] For a synchronous machine having impedance angle \(\theta\), \[P_m = \frac{E_fV}{|Z_s|} - \frac{E_f^2}{|Z_s|}\cos\theta\] Substituting \[P_m=2.5,\qquad V=1,\qquad |Z_s|=0.3162,\qquad \theta=71.56^\circ\] \[2.5 = \frac{E_f(1)}{0.3162} - \frac{E_f^2}{0.3162}\cos(71.56^\circ)\] Since \[\cos(71.56^\circ)\approx 0.3162\] \[2.5 = 3.162E_f-E_f^2\] \[E_f^2-3.162E_f+2.5=0\] Solving, \[E_f = \frac{3.162\pm\sqrt{(3.162)^2-4(2.5)}}{2}\] \[E_f = 1.58\] Taking the required value, \[\boxed{1.58}\]
Key points
  • Convert the synchronous impedance into polar form before applying the power equation.
  • Maximum developed power occurs when the load angle equals the impedance angle, i.e., \[\delta=\theta.\]
  • For a synchronous machine with non-zero resistance, \[P_m=\frac{E_fV}{|Z_s|}\cos(\theta-\delta)-\frac{E_f^2}{|Z_s|}\cos\theta.\]
  • At maximum power condition, \[P_{m,\max}=\frac{E_fV}{|Z_s|}-\frac{E_f^2}{|Z_s|}\cos\theta.\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use only the reactance value; use the magnitude of \(Z_s\).
  • Do not forget to convert \(Z_s\) into polar form.
  • For maximum power transfer, use \(\delta=\theta\), not \(\delta=90^\circ\).
  • Check the quadratic roots carefully before selecting the final answer.

questions.question: A balanced delta connected load consisting of the series connection of one resistor (\(R=15~\Omega\)) and a capacitor (\(C=212.21~\mu\text{F}\)) in each phase is connected to three-phase, \(50~\text{Hz}\), \(415~\text{V}\) supply terminals through a line having an inductance of \(L=31.83~\text{mH}\) per phase, as shown in figure below. Considering the change in the supply terminal voltage with loading to be negligible, the magnitude of the voltage across the terminals \(V_{AB}\) in volts is [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
Method 1
The line reactance is \[X_L=2\pi fL =2\pi(50)(31.83\times10^{-3}) =10~\Omega\] Hence, \[Z_{line}=j10~\Omega\] The capacitive reactance is \[X_C=\frac{1}{2\pi fC} = \frac{1}{2\pi(50)(212.21\times10^{-6})} = 15~\Omega\] Therefore, \[Z_{\Delta} = 15-j15~\Omega\] [figure unavailable] Converting the balanced delta load into an equivalent star, \[Z_Y = \frac{Z_\Delta}{3} = 5-j5~\Omega\] The per-phase equivalent circuit is shown below. [figure unavailable] The phase voltage across the equivalent load is \[V_{AN} = \frac{5-j5}{(5-j5)+j10} \times \frac{415}{\sqrt3}\] \[= \frac{5-j5}{5+j5} \times \frac{415}{\sqrt3}\] Since \[\left| \frac{5-j5}{5+j5} \right| =1\] \[|V_{AN}| = \frac{415}{\sqrt3}\] Hence, \[|V_{AB}| = \sqrt3\,|V_{AN}| = 415~V\]
Method 2
Let the load phase voltage be \(V_{AB}\). For a balanced delta load, \[I_{AB}=\frac{V_{AB}}{15-j15}\] Applying KVL between source terminals A and B, \[V_{AB,\text{source}} = V_{AB} + j10\,(I_A-I_B)\] For a balanced delta, \[I_A-I_B=3I_{AB}\] Hence, \[V_{AB,\text{source}} = V_{AB} + 3j10\,I_{AB}\] Substituting \[I_{AB} = \frac{V_{AB}}{15-j15}\] gives \[V_{AB,\text{source}} = V_{AB} \left( 1+\frac{j30}{15-j15} \right)\] Now, \[\frac{j30}{15-j15} = -1+j\] Therefore, \[1+\frac{j30}{15-j15} = j\] Hence, \[V_{AB,\text{source}} = jV_{AB}\] Taking magnitudes, \[|V_{AB,\text{source}}| = |V_{AB}|\] Since \[|V_{AB,\text{source}}| = 415\,\text{V}\] we obtain \[|V_{AB}| = 415\,\text{V}\] Therefore, the correct answer is \[\boxed{V_{AB}=415~V}\]

questions.question: The two-bus power system shown in figure (i) has one alternator supplying a synchronous motor load through a Y-\(\Delta\) transformer. The positive, negative and zero-sequence diagrams of the system are shown in figures (ii), (iii) and (iv), respectively. All reactances in the sequence diagrams are in p.u. If a bolted line-to-line fault (fault impedance = zero) between phases `\(b\)' and `\(c\)' at bus \(1\), neglecting the pre-fault currents, the magnitude of the fault current (from phase `\(b\)' to `\(c\)') in p.u. is (Round off to \(2\) decimal places). [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] Step 1: Recall fault current relation for an L-L fault.
For a line-to-line fault, the zero-sequence network is not involved. The positive- and negative-sequence networks are connected in parallel. \[I_f = \sqrt{3}\,|I_{a1}|\] where \[I_{a1} = \frac{E}{Z_1 + Z_2}\] Here, \[Z_1 = \text{positive-sequence Thevenin impedance at bus }1\] and \[Z_2 = \text{negative-sequence Thevenin impedance at bus }1\] Step 2: Positive-sequence impedance.
From figure (ii), the equivalent positive-sequence impedance seen from bus \(1\) is: \[Z_1 = \left( \frac{j0.2 \times j0.3}{j0.2 + j0.3} \right) = j0.12\] Step 3: Negative-sequence impedance.
From figure (iii), similarly, \[Z_2 = \left( \frac{j0.2 \times j0.3}{j0.2 + j0.3} \right) = j0.12\] Step 4: Prefault voltage.
Neglecting pre-fault currents, \[E = 1.0\,\text{p.u.}\] Step 5: Sequence current.
\[I_{a1} = \frac{1}{j0.12 + j0.12} = \frac{1}{j0.24} = -j4.167\] Hence, \[|I_{a1}| = 4.167\,\text{p.u.}\] Step 6: Fault current.
\[I_f = \sqrt{3}\times 4.167 = 7.2168\,\text{p.u.}\] \[\boxed{7.21}\]
Key points
  • For an L-L fault, only positive- and negative-sequence networks participate.
  • Zero-sequence network is not involved in a line-to-line fault.
  • Fault current relation: \[I_f = \sqrt{3}\,|I_{a1}|\]
  • Neglecting pre-fault current implies prefault voltage of \(1\,\text{p.u.}\).

questions.ref: Power System Matrices and Load Flow Q1
questions.question:
The bus admittance (\(Y_{\text{bus}}\)) matrix of a \(3\)-bus power system is given below. \[Y_{\text{bus}}=
\begin{bmatrix}
-j15 & j10 & j5\\
j10 & -j13.5 & j4\\
j5 & j4 & -j8
\end{bmatrix}\] Considering that there is no shunt inductor connected to any of the buses, which of the following can NOT be true?
options: Line charging capacitor of finite value is present in all three lines
Line charging capacitor of finite value is present in line \(2\)--\(3\) only
Line charging capacitor of finite value is present in line \(2\)--\(3\) only and shunt capacitor of finite value is present in bus \(1\) only
Line charging capacitor of finite value is present in line \(2\)--\(3\) only and shunt capacitor of finite value is present in bus \(3\) only
questions.explanation:
Recall the properties of the bus admittance matrix: \[Y_{ij} = -Y_{\text{line}(i,j)}, \qquad i \neq j\] and \[Y_{ii} = \sum_{j \neq i} Y_{\text{line}(i,j)} + Y_{\text{shunt},i}\] From the off-diagonal entries: \[Y_{12}=j10 \Rightarrow Y_{\text{line}(1,2)}=-j10\] \[Y_{13}=j5 \Rightarrow Y_{\text{line}(1,3)}=-j5\] \[Y_{23}=j4 \Rightarrow Y_{\text{line}(2,3)}=-j4\] Thus, all the three transmission lines \((1\)--\(2)\), \((1\)--\(3)\) and \((2\)--\(3)\) are present. Now compare the diagonal entries with the sum of corresponding line admittances. For bus \(1\): \[Y_{11}=-j15\] Expected from connected lines: \[-(j10+j5)=-j15\] Hence, no additional shunt element is connected at bus \(1\). For bus \(2\): \[Y_{22}=-j13.5\] Expected from connected lines: \[-(j10+j4)=-j14\] Difference: \[-j13.5-(-j14)=j0.5\] Hence, a shunt capacitive contribution exists at bus \(2\). For bus \(3\): \[Y_{33}=-j8\] Expected from connected lines: \[-(j5+j4)=-j9\] Difference: \[-j8-(-j9)=j1\] Hence, a shunt capacitive contribution exists at bus \(3\). Therefore, it is not possible that only line \(2\)--\(3\) has line charging capacitance, because the off-diagonal terms clearly indicate the presence of all three lines. \[\boxed{\text{(B) Line charging capacitor of finite value is present in line 2--3 only}}\]
Key points
  • Off-diagonal element \(Y_{ij}\) equals the negative of the admittance between buses \(i\) and \(j\).
  • Any mismatch between a diagonal entry and the negative sum of corresponding off-diagonal terms indicates shunt admittance.
  • Positive imaginary correction in diagonal entries indicates capacitive shunt contribution.

questions.question: The three-bus power system shown in the figure has one alternator connected to bus \(2\) which supplies \(200\,\text{MW}\) and \(40\,\text{MVAr}\) power. Bus \(3\) is infinite bus having a voltage of magnitude \(|V_3| = 1.0\,\text{p.u.}\) and angle of \(-15^\circ\). A variable current source, \(|I|\angle\phi\) is connected at bus \(1\) and controlled such that the magnitude of the bus \(1\) voltage is maintained at \(1.05\,\text{p.u.}\) and the phase angle of the source current, \(\phi = \theta_1 \pm \frac{\pi}{2}\), where \(\theta_1\) is the phase angle of the bus \(1\) voltage. The three buses can be categorized for load flow analysis as
options:
Bus \(1\) Slack bus
Bus \(2\) \(P-|V|\) bus
Bus \(3\) \(P-Q\) bus

Bus \(1\) \(P-|V|\) bus
Bus \(2\) \(P-|V|\) bus
Bus \(3\) Slack bus

Bus \(1\) \(P-Q\) bus
Bus \(2\) \(P-Q\) bus
Bus \(3\) Slack bus

Bus \(1\) \(P-|V|\) bus
Bus \(2\) \(P-Q\) bus
Bus \(3\) Slack bus
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify bus 3 (infinite bus).
Bus \(3\) is specified as an infinite bus with: \[|V_3| = 1.0\,\text{p.u.}, \qquad \delta_3 = -15^\circ\] Since both voltage magnitude and phase angle are specified, bus \(3\) is the slack bus. Step 2: Identify bus 2 (alternator bus).
At bus \(2\), the alternator supplies: \[P_2 = 200\,\text{MW}\] \[Q_2 = 40\,\text{MVAr}\] Thus, both active and reactive powers are specified. Hence, bus \(2\) is a \(P-Q\) bus. Step 3: Identify bus 1 (controlled current source bus).
At bus \(1\), the voltage magnitude is maintained at: \[|V_1| = 1.05\,\text{p.u.}\] Also, \[\phi = \theta_1 \pm \frac{\pi}{2}\] This implies that the injected current is in quadrature with the bus voltage. Therefore, the current source controls reactive power injection while the voltage magnitude is specified. Hence, bus \(1\) is a \(P-|V|\) bus. Step 4: Final categorization.
\[\boxed{ \text{(D) \enspace Bus 1: } P-|V| \text{ bus, \quad Bus 2: } P-Q \text{ bus, \quad Bus 3: Slack bus} }\]
Key points
  • Slack bus: both voltage magnitude and phase angle are specified.
  • \(P-Q\) bus: active and reactive powers are specified.
  • \(P-|V|\) bus: active power and voltage magnitude are specified.
  • Infinite bus is always treated as the slack bus in load flow analysis.

questions.subject: power-electronics
questions.question: The circuit shown in the figure has reached steady state with thyristor \(T\) in the OFF condition. Assume that the latching and holding currents of the thyristor are zero. The thyristor is turned ON at \(t=0\,\mathrm{s}\). The duration in microseconds for which the thyristor would conduct before it turns OFF is (Round off to two decimal places). [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
Initially, the capacitor is charged to the supply voltage: \[V_C = V_s = 100\,\text{V}.\] When thyristor \(T\) is triggered, the capacitor discharges through the resonant \(LC\) loop. The resonant conduction time for one half-cycle is \[t_1 = \pi\sqrt{LC}.\] The peak resonant current is \[I_p = V_s\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} = 100\sqrt{\frac{1\,\mu\text{F}}{4\,\mu\text{H}}} = 50\,\text{A}.\] The load current is \[I_0 = \frac{V_s}{R} = \frac{100}{4} = 25\,\text{A}.\] [figure unavailable] The thyristor turns OFF when the total current becomes zero: \[0 = \frac{V_s}{R} - I_p\sin(\omega_0 t_2).\] \[\omega_0 t_2 = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{I_0}{I_p}\right) = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{25}{50}\right) = \frac{\pi}{6}.\] Thus, \[t_2 = \frac{\pi}{6}\sqrt{LC}.\] Total thyristor conduction time is \[t_{\text{total}} = t_1 + t_2 = \pi\sqrt{LC} + \frac{\pi}{6}\sqrt{LC} = \frac{7\pi}{6}\sqrt{LC}.\] Substituting the given values, \[t_{\text{total}} = \frac{7\pi}{6}\sqrt{(1 \times 10^{-6})(4 \times 10^{-6})} = \frac{7\pi}{3} \times 10^{-6}\,\text{s}.\] \[t_{\text{total}} \approx 7.33\,\mu\text{s}.\] \[\boxed{7.33}\]
Key points
  • Resonant discharge through an \(LC\) circuit gives a half-cycle conduction time of \(\pi\sqrt{LC}\).
  • Total thyristor conduction time is obtained by adding the resonant interval and current decay interval.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not stop the calculation at only \(\pi\sqrt{LC}\) when load current is also present.
  • Keep the final NAT answer numerical only.

questions.question: The single phase rectifier consisting of three thyristors \(T_1\), \(T_2\), \(T_3\) and a diode \(D_1\) feed power to a \(10\,\mathrm{A}\) constant current load. \(T_1\) and \(T_3\) are fired at \(\alpha = 60^\circ\) and \(T_2\) is fired at \(\alpha = 240^\circ\). The reference for \(\alpha\) is the positive zero crossing of \(V_{in}\). The average voltage \(V_o\) across the load in volts is (Round off to 2 decimal places). [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] The average output voltage \(V_o\) is given by integrating the voltage waveform over its periodic interval: \[V_o = \frac{1}{2\pi} \left[ \int_{\alpha}^{\pi} V_m \sin\omega t \, d(\omega t) + \int_{\pi+\alpha}^{2\pi+\alpha} -V_m \sin\omega t \, d(\omega t) \right]\] Evaluating the integrals simplifies to the following expression: \[V_o = \frac{V_m}{2\pi} [1 + 3\cos\alpha]\] Given parameters from the problem context:
  • Peak voltage, \(V_m = 100\,\text{V}\)
  • Firing angle, \(\alpha = 60^\circ\)
Substituting these values into the average voltage equation: \[V_o = \frac{100}{2\pi} [1 + 3\cos 60^\circ] = \frac{100}{2\pi} \left[1 + 3(0.5)\right] = \frac{250}{2\pi} \approx 39.78\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{39.78}\]
Key points
  • From \(\pi\) to \(\pi+\alpha\), \(T_3\) and \(D_1\) will perform freewheeling action of the load current, hence output voltage will be \(0\).
